paragraphs.heading: A matrix with an inverse
paragraphs.text: An invertible matrix is a square matrix that has an inverse; it is also called non-singular, non-degenerate or regular. An n × n matrix A is invertible when some n × n matrix B gives AB = BA = Iₙ, where Iₙ is the n × n identity matrix. That B is fixed uniquely by A, is called the inverse of A, and is written A⁻¹. A matrix and its inverse are always the same size.

paragraphs.heading: Undoing a move
paragraphs.text: The inverse undoes what the matrix does. Apply a matrix to a vector and then apply its inverse, and you get the original vector back. Seen as a transformation, a matrix is invertible when another linear transformation can reverse it. Then applying A and A⁻¹, in either order, returns every vector to where it began.

paragraphs.heading: No squashing
paragraphs.text: Geometrically, an invertible matrix never squashes space into a set with fewer dimensions. It keeps different vectors different and reaches every vector in the target space. For a real matrix the determinant shows this: an invertible matrix has a nonzero determinant, while a determinant of zero means the matrix shrinks volume to zero and has no inverse.

paragraphs.heading: Many equivalent tests
paragraphs.text: Many tests for invertibility turn out to be equivalent, and the invertible matrix theorem gathers them together. A matrix is invertible exactly when the only solution of A x = 0 is the zero vector, so its nullspace holds nothing else. An n × n matrix is also invertible when its rank is n, and such a matrix is said to have full rank. Another test is that its determinant is not zero.

paragraphs.heading: Finding the inverse
paragraphs.text: A practical test comes from row reduction. A square matrix is invertible exactly when its row-reduced echelon form is the identity matrix. The same idea computes the inverse with Gaussian elimination: place the matrix beside the identity matrix in one augmented matrix, then row-reduce until the left half becomes the identity. At that point the right half has become the inverse.

paragraphs.heading: Singular matrices
paragraphs.text: Over a field, a square matrix without an inverse is called singular or degenerate. A zero determinant is both necessary and sufficient for this. Over a commutative ring, the rule changes slightly: a square matrix is invertible exactly when its determinant is a unit, meaning an element that has its own multiplicative inverse.
